rationale: A wins because it gives the founder three genuinely different doors into the story and names the proof needed before anyone starts pitching. Its platform angle, "Mindbody Owns the Studio Software, the Consumer Marketplace, and Now the AI That Fills Both," is overcaffeinated but strategically useful because it turns ClassPass from trivia into a reportable tension. B is solid, but "The boutique-fitness booking platform is now placing software between studios and their schedules" stretches "suggests optimal class times" into "software decides the schedule," and that is how a decent pitch becomes a fact-check problem.
gaps_in_A: "Rolling Out to 50,000 Studios" overstates the supplied fact. The update says Mindbody powers booking for over 50,000 studios and salons, not that this assistant is rolling out to all of them.
"While Fitness Apps Race to Build AI Coaches" invents a broader market race that was not in the update. Useful frame, bad unsupported peg.

"the AI That Fills Both" implies the assistant sits across Mindbody and ClassPass before the ClassPass relationship is proven. The proof section admits this hole, but the headline spends the check first.
"defensible moat" is analyst-deck language unless Mindbody can prove data access, switching costs, or ClassPass interaction. Otherwise it is strategy fog.
gaps_in_B: "cut studio no-show rates 22% by texting the waitlist" attributes the whole pilot result to texting, but the update does not isolate texting from the scheduling recommendations.
"software decides the schedule" overstates the actual fact, which is that the assistant suggests optimal class times. Suggesting is not deciding.
"using aggregated booking data across the network" invents the data scope. The update only says booking data, not network-wide aggregation.
"founder/category/competitor cuts below" is template shrapnel. There is no founder angle and no real competitor angle, so it undercuts the claimed distinctness.
